evals.prompt: I want to connect my Google Search Console so I can see how my site does in search. I'm not technical.
evals.expected_output: Should run the onboarding wizard, not dump commands. Must explain the BENEFIT first (real queries, positions, free, read-only) and ask 'want to connect now?' before any setup. Must check what's already done (token/creds/venv) and only ask for what's missing. Must clearly flag the human-only Google-console steps (enable API, Google Auth Platform → Audience → Test user, create Desktop OAuth client, download JSON) as 'you do this', one at a time, and the agent-side steps (move JSON, build venv, first run) as 'I do this'. Must use a venv (not bare pip) and confirm the connection in plain words once done, then teach how to use it.
assertions: Explains the benefit BEFORE asking for setup steps
Asks for confirmation before starting setup
Checks existing token/creds/venv and skips already-done steps
Flags the human-only Google-console clicks separately from agent steps
References Google Auth Platform → Audience → Test users (not the old 'OAuth consent screen' path)
Uses a virtualenv, not a bare 'pip install'
Confirms connection in plain language and then explains how to use it

evals.prompt: Where do I rank for 'AI events in Munich'? And what are my quickest SEO wins?
evals.expected_output: Should run gsc_query.py (via the venv) for the verified property with the keyword, and report the keyword's current average position plus the striking-distance queries (avg position ~8-20) as the fastest Top-10 wins. Should also surface high-impression/low-CTR pages as snippet/SERP investigation targets (title/meta rewrites only after the live-SERP check). Should honestly state if the property is too new / near-empty rather than inventing data.
assertions: Runs gsc_query.py through the venv python
Reports the target keyword's average position
Surfaces striking-distance queries (pos ~8-20) as quick wins
Flags high-impression / low-CTR pages as snippet/SERP investigation targets, not automatic title/meta rewrites
Honestly reports a near-empty property instead of fabricating data

evals.prompt: How do I rank on Bing, and is my site visible to Copilot/ChatGPT?
evals.expected_output: Should run bing_query.py (which uses the simple BING_API_KEY, not OAuth) and report Bing positions for the target keywords, framing Bing as a proxy for Copilot/ChatGPT visibility. Should note Bing volume is much smaller than Google. If no BING_API_KEY is set, should explain the ~2-minute API-key setup (Bing Webmaster Tools → Settings → API Access) and that one key covers all sites, without blocking the Google data.
assertions: Runs bing_query.py (API key, not OAuth)
Reports Bing keyword positions
Frames Bing as a Copilot/ChatGPT visibility proxy
Notes Bing volume is smaller than Google
If no key: explains the API-key setup and that it's account-wide, without blocking GSC

evals.prompt: My site gets very little traffic. How should I actually use this data to improve?
evals.expected_output: Should apply the low-volume playbook: track POSITION and impressions rather than clicks (clicks are noisy at low volume); convert striking-distance queries one at a time; fix titles for queries that rank but don't get clicked (after the live-SERP check confirms a controllable snippet problem); mine the unexpected queries the site already appears for; and use the SERP + Bing layers to find weak-competition / long-tail / other-language terms. Should recommend re-measuring every 1-2 weeks, not daily, and comparing windows.
assertions: Says to track position/impressions, not clicks, at low volume
Recommends converting striking-distance queries one at a time
Recommends the live-SERP check before fixing titles for ranked-but-unclicked queries
Suggests mining unexpected/long-tail queries the site already appears for
Recommends a weekly/biweekly cadence rather than daily

evals.prompt: Is my position for these keywords improving over time? Set me up to watch it.
evals.expected_output: Should use track.sh (or gsc_query.py/bing_query.py with --csv) to append the run to the history CSV and print the week-over-week position trend via _history.py, explaining that lower position is better and a drop in the number is an improvement (shown as ▲). On the first run it should say there's no prior data yet and to re-run in 1-2 weeks. Should NOT claim a trend exists from a single data point.
assertions: Uses track.sh or the --csv flag to record history
Prints/explains a week-over-week position trend
Explains lower position = better (improvement is a drop in the number)
On first run, states there is no prior data yet rather than inventing a trend

evals.prompt: My GSC report shows 123 impressions for one query and a query-level total of 384 impressions site-wide, but the page-level table's rows actually sum to 1,071. Which total should I use, and is 'this query is 32% of site-wide traffic' a correct claim? Also, one of my pages ranks position 4 with 0% CTR at 150 impressions, and a --query drill-down confirms the 123-impression query lands only on that page — what does that mean, and what should I check before rewriting its title?
evals.expected_output: Should explain that NEITHER sum is the true site-wide figure: the query-level total (384) undercounts (anonymization drops rare queries) and the page-level sum (1,071) overcounts (each page is counted separately when several share one results page, e.g. brand sitelinks) — the correct denominator is the property-level (no-dimension) total, which the report prints. Best answer reframes the claim page-relative (123 of the page's own 150 impressions, ~82%) instead of any site-wide percentage. Should read position ~4 with ~0% CTR as a snippet OR SERP-context problem (a knowledge panel or Wikipedia can absorb clicks on an entity query), decided by the mandatory live-SERP check (serp_check.py) against the page's actual shipped meta description before any title/description rewrite.
assertions: Does NOT bless the page-level sum (1,071) as the true site-wide figure — explains it can overcount (pages counted separately per results page)
Flags the query-level total as an anonymized undercount, not a valid denominator
Names the property-level (no-dimension) total as the correct site-wide denominator, or reframes the claim page-relative (123/150, using the attribution the drill-down established)
Reads position ~4 + ~0% CTR as snippet-or-SERP-context, not automatically a snippet defect and not a ranking problem
States the live-SERP-snippet check (serp_check.py) is mandatory before recommending a title/description rewrite

evals.prompt: Great news I think? My tracker shows 'ai tools' improved ▲ +2.1 this week (4 impressions), my top query jumped to 210 impressions (it's my company's name), and impressions are up 40% versus the report I saved last month — I changed my homepage title two weeks ago, so it clearly worked. Should I roll the same title pattern out to every page?
evals.expected_output: Should decline the causal leap and check each number's meaning first: a ▲ on ~4 impressions is noise (and the tracker may have matched a different query — check the ≠/~ markers); the brand-name query says nothing about SEO progress and must be separated from non-brand rows before quoting growth; the 40% comparison mixes a fresh pull against a stale saved report — re-pull both windows from the same source with equal lengths and name them. Before crediting the title change, compare equal windows and look at pages that were NOT changed as a control, and say 'consistent with' rather than 'it worked'. No rollout recommendation until non-brand, equal-window, controlled evidence supports it.
assertions: Treats a position move on ~4 impressions as noise, not a win (and mentions the changed-query/thin-data markers)
Separates the brand-name query from non-brand before any growth claim
Rejects comparing a fresh pull against a stale saved report — demands equal, named windows from the same source
Requires a control (unchanged pages, equal windows) before attributing anything to the title change
Does not recommend the site-wide rollout on this evidence
